blocks.title: Data States, Sovereignty, and Geolocation comparison
Data States, Sovereignty, and Geolocation exam shortcuts
items: Stored on disk → DATA AT REST
Protect stored data with controls such as encryption and permissions.
Moving across a network → DATA IN TRANSIT
Protect communications with TLS, VPNs, or IPsec.
Example: HTTPS traffic between browser and server.
Decrypted and being processed → DATA IN USE
The data is active in memory or an application.
Example: A payroll record displayed in an application.
Law depends on storage region → DATA SOVEREIGNTY
Jurisdiction can determine legal and compliance requirements.
Example: Customer data stored in another country.
Question asks where data resides → GEOLOCATION
Focus on the actual region or location.
Example: A cloud workload must remain in a specified country.
blocks.example: Focus on what the scenario is protecting: confidentiality, integrity, access, location, or legal handling requirements.

questions.q: A database backup is stored on disk and is not being transmitted. Which data state is this?
questions.explanation: Stored data that is not moving is data at rest.

questions.q: A user accesses a website over HTTPS. Which data state is being protected while the packets cross the network?
questions.explanation: Data moving between systems is data in transit.

questions.q: A decrypted payroll record is currently loaded in application memory. Which data state is this?
questions.explanation: Data actively being processed in memory is data in use.

questions.q: A company must store customer records inside a particular country because local law applies to the data. Which concept is most relevant?
questions.explanation: Data sovereignty concerns the laws of the jurisdiction where data is stored or processed.

questions.q: A cloud administrator needs to know which geographic region currently hosts a workload. Which concept is most direct?
questions.explanation: Geolocation identifies the actual physical or logical location of systems or data.
